annotations.keyFindings: Across 9,800 patient-shifts on four geriatric wards, 58 percent had a completed screen: 71 percent on days, 62 percent on evenings and 39 percent on nights, and 11 points lower at weekends.
annotations.limitations: Record reconciliation without direct observation; four wards in one region.

annotations.keyFindings: Of screens documented in the record, 17 percent had not been performed when observed, mostly at night and for sleeping patients.
annotations.limitations: Two wards; observers may have changed behaviour on sampled shifts.

annotations.keyFindings: A shift-start prompt was followed by completion rising from 52 to 74 percent, least at night; time to medical review did not change.
annotations.limitations: Concurrent staffing change on one ward; single system.

annotations.keyFindings: Patients with dementia were screened on 41 percent of shifts against 66 percent without dementia; severe sensory loss 48 percent.
annotations.limitations: Record-based; dementia diagnosis taken from the notes.

annotations.keyFindings: Nurses rated time at shift start, perceived futility and uncertainty with dementia as the main barriers.
annotations.limitations: Self-rated barriers; response rate not reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Only 38 percent of positive screens were reviewed by a doctor within 24 hours; night and weekend screens waited longest.
annotations.limitations: Two wards; review taken from documentation.

claims.text: On four acute geriatric wards, delirium screening was completed on 71 percent of day shifts, 62 percent of evening shifts and 39 percent of night shifts.
claims.passage: Completion was 71 percent on day shifts, 62 percent on evening shifts and 39 percent on night shifts
claims.interpretation: Shift type is the first stratifier to measure; the local June check points the same way.

claims.text: In 17 percent of documented delirium screens the screening questions had not been asked.
claims.passage: in 17 percent a screen was documented but the questions were not asked
claims.interpretation: Record reconciliation alone overestimates completion; a sample of direct observation is needed.

claims.text: Patients with dementia were screened on 41 percent of shifts compared with 66 percent of shifts for patients without dementia.
claims.passage: Patients with a recorded dementia diagnosis had screens on 41 percent of shifts, compared with 66 percent for patients without dementia.
claims.interpretation: Dementia is a pre-specified patient group for the local study.

claims.text: Only 38 percent of positive delirium screens led to a documented medical review within 24 hours.
claims.passage: Thirty-eight percent were reviewed within 24 hours
claims.interpretation: Measure the step from a positive screen to review alongside completion.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Studies on geriatric wards consistently report that screening completion is lowest at night and at weekends, and lowest for people with dementia or sensory loss, who are at the highest risk of delirium. Record review overstates screening because some documented screens were never performed. Positive screens often wait more than a day for medical review. A prompt raised completion in one time series but not at night and not the step to review. The pattern supports measuring completion per patient-shift with a sample of direct observation before choosing a fix.
gradeRationale: Consistent observational findings across several wards and methods for where screening fails; moderate certainty for the pattern, low for the effect of any single fix.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty moderate.
